statement: In people prescribed benzodiazepine sleeping pills, observational studies summarized second-hand in a narrative review (Vermeeren, 2004) found more injurious road crashes than without them, mostly in the first weeks after a new prescription (odds ratio 6.5, 95% CI 1.9 to 22.5, in the first two weeks, falling to 1.4 in the second month, in one Canadian cohort), but no clear increase for sleeping pills in a UK case-crossover study (odds ratio 1.2, 0.8 to 1.7) or in one study of older drivers (0.9, 0.4 to 2.0), and in another study of drivers over 65 an increase only for longer-acting benzodiazepines in the first week (1.5, 1.0 to 2.0); in older people, a meta-analysis of 40 studies found about 1.5 times the odds of falls with sedatives and sleeping pills, with risks highest in the first weeks of use and higher with larger doses; in nursing homes, falls were more common with any benzodiazepine. These associations may partly reflect why the pills were prescribed (confounding by indication), and the figures are second-hand. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Crashes and falls were more common in people who had just started sleeping pills in some studies, but not in others, and the studies cannot prove the pills caused them.
population: People prescribed benzodiazepine sleeping pills in Canada, the UK and the US (cohort, case-crossover and case-control studies published from the 1970s to about 2002), including adults over 65
exposure: Use of a benzodiazepine sleeping pill, especially in the weeks after a new prescription
comparator: People or periods without such use
outcome: Injurious road crashes; falls and hip fractures in older people
magnitude: Crashes: odds ratio 6.5 (95% CI 1.9 to 22.5) in weeks 1 to 2 and 3.9 (1.9 to 8.3) in weeks 1 to 4 after a new prescription, 1.4 in the second month (Saskatchewan cohort); 1.2 (0.8 to 1.7) for hypnotics in a UK case-crossover study; 1.0 (0.8 to 1.3) for shorter-acting and 1.5 (1.0 to 2.0) for longer-acting benzodiazepines in the first week in drivers over 65; 0.9 (0.4 to 2.0) in another study of older drivers. Falls in older people: pooled odds ratios 1.54 (sedatives and hypnotics) and 1.48 (benzodiazepines) in a meta-analysis of 40 studies; rate ratios 3.0 in week 1, 2.2 in weeks 2 to 4 and 1.3 later in nursing-home residents.

evidence.locator: 3.1 Traffic Accidents, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table II, row Neutel
evidence.extracted: In a Saskatchewan cohort of 225 796 people prescribed benzodiazepines and 97 862 controls, the odds ratio for an injurious crash after a hypnotic prescription was 6.5 (95% CI 1.9 to 22.5) in weeks 1 to 2 and 3.9 (1.9 to 8.3) in weeks 1 to 4, falling to 1.4 in weeks 5 to 8; 3.2 (1.4 to 7.3) for triazolam and 5.1 (2.3 to 11.6) for flurazepam in weeks 1 to 4.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

evidence.locator: 3.1, right column, 1st paragraph; Table II, row Barbone et al.
evidence.extracted: In a UK case-crossover study of 19 386 drivers in a first traffic accident, comparing each driver's periods with and without exposure, the odds ratio was 1.2 (95% CI 0.8 to 1.7) for hypnotics and 2.2 (1.5 to 3.1) for anxiolytic benzodiazepines; zopiclone, the only short half-life hypnotic, had an odds ratio of 4.0.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

evidence.locator: Table II, rows Hemmelgarn et al. and Leveille et al.
evidence.extracted: In a nested case-control study of drivers aged 65 or over (5579 injurious crashes, 13 256 controls), odds ratios were 1.0 (0.8 to 1.3) for benzodiazepines with half-lives of 24 hours or less and 1.5 (1.0 to 2.0) for longer ones in week 1 of use; in a matched case-control study of older drivers (234 injurious crashes, 447 controls), 0.9 (0.4 to 2.0) for benzodiazepines, mostly flurazepam and triazolam.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

evidence.locator: 3.2 Risk of Falling and Hip Fracture, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: A meta-analysis of 40 epidemiological studies of falls in the elderly gave pooled odds ratios of 1.54 for sedatives and hypnotics and 1.48 for benzodiazepines, with risks varying considerably between studies.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

evidence.extracted: Risks of fall-related injury were highest at the start of treatment: odds ratio 3.6 in the first two weeks, 2.3 in weeks 3 and 4 and 1.4 in the second month after a hypnotic prescription; in nursing-home residents using benzodiazepines, adjusted rate ratios for falls of 3.0 in week 1, 2.2 in weeks 2 to 4 and 1.3 in the second month.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

evidence.extracted: The author notes that epidemiological data show statistical associations rather than causality, that the effects of the illness are hard to separate from those of the medicine, and that prescribing safer drugs to frailer patients can mask differences.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

risk_of_bias.note: Observational studies with confounding by indication and exposure misclassification, as the author notes; not appraisable from the review.

inconsistency.note: Some studies found clear increases and others none; risks varied considerably between studies.

indirectness.note: Second-hand figures from a narrative review; studies from the 1970s to about 2002, partly of drugs now less prescribed.

large_effect.note: Not applied: estimates come second-hand from unadjusted or variably adjusted observational studies.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness (second-hand), which leaves very low. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). Status mixed: the crash studies disagree. The primary studies (Neutel; Barbone et al.; Hemmelgarn et al.; Leipzig et al.) are the sources to read before this claim can rise.
